lesson.title: One of Each: Removing Duplicates with Sets
lesson.summary: Passing a list to set() collapses it down to its unique elements in one step, because a set can never contain the same value twice.
lesson.body:
The Sets chapter established a defining rule about sets: every element in a set is unique, and Python enforces this automatically. If you try to add a value that's already present, nothing changes. This rule turns out to be a remarkably convenient tool for a very common task, since Lists, unlike sets, allow duplicate values without complaint, and real data is full of repeats, survey responses with the same answer twice, a log file with the same error recorded many times, a spreadsheet column with repeated entries.

To strip duplicates out of a list, pass it to the set() constructor. Python walks through the list and builds a set containing each distinct value exactly once, silently dropping every repeat.

scores = [88, 92, 88, 75, 92, 100]
unique_scores = set(scores)
print(len(unique_scores))
print(sorted(unique_scores))

len(unique_scores) prints 4, since 88 and 92 each appeared twice in the original list of six numbers, leaving four distinct values. sorted(unique_scores) then prints [75, 88, 92, 100], a clean, ordered list of what remained. Sorting is used here for a predictable, readable result, since a set does not remember the order elements were inserted in the way a list does.

If you need the deduplicated result back as a list, wrap the set() call in list(): unique_list = list(set(scores)). Be aware that this specific conversion does not guarantee the original order is preserved, since the values pass through a set along the way, so if you need the original order kept intact with duplicates removed, set() alone isn't quite enough, and you'd need a small loop or a different tool to track what you've already seen. Still, when all you need is the collection of distinct values and order doesn't matter, set(some_list) is the single fastest and most readable way to get there, and it's one of the most common practical reasons Python programmers reach for a set in the first place.
